cover.title: Docker Complete Handbook
cover.subtitle: From Basics to Advanced
cover.tagline: One image, same app on laptop, CI and production

items: The `docker` CLI is only a ==client==; it does no container work
It sends REST calls to the `dockerd` daemon
Default endpoint: unix socket `/var/run/docker.sock`
Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows hides `dockerd` in a Linux VM
Reason: containers need a **Linux** kernel
`dockerd` hands lifecycle and images to ==containerd==
containerd calls ==runc==, the OCI runtime that creates the container
`containerd-shim` stays as the parent of the process
Shim keeps the container alive if dockerd or containerd restarts

rows: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup

items: ==overlay2== stacks read-only image layers under one writable layer
The container only ever writes to the top layer
==OCI== specs fix the image format and runtime
So one image runs on Docker, Podman or containerd

blocks.text: 5. Example: docker run alpine echo hi

lines: # raw REST, same API as the CLI
blocks.note: The CLI is just an HTTP client

items: Mounting `docker.sock` into a container: **root-equivalent** control of the host
Blaming dockerd restarts for dead containers; the shim keeps them running
Expecting a container to outlive its PID 1: when PID 1 exits, the container stops

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What does runc do?
How do namespaces differ from cgroups?
Why does a container die when its PID 1 exits?
All containers share **one** host kernel
A kernel exploit can reach every container
VMs boot a guest OS, so isolation is stronger

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: A container is a kernel-isolated process: dockerd → containerd → shim → runc, with namespaces limiting what it sees and cgroups limiting what it uses.

items: An ==image== is an immutable stack of layers plus a JSON config
The config holds env, entrypoint, cmd and exposed ports
RUN, COPY and ADD change the filesystem, so each makes a {green:layer}
ENV and CMD only edit the config, not the files
Each layer is named by its ==SHA256 digest==, a hash of its bytes
Identical layers are stored **once** and shared across images
A tag like `nginx:1.27` is a movable pointer
A digest like `nginx@sha256:...` is {blue:immutable}
Layers below are read-only; the container adds a writable layer
Editing a lower file ==copies it up== into that layer first
Deleting a file in a later layer only **hides** it
The bytes still ship in the earlier layer, so size never shrinks

lines: # one row per layer with SIZE
blocks.note: History lists layers; inspect lists config

items: **:latest** in production makes deploys non-reproducible
Secrets or build caches left in a layer
They stay recoverable with `docker history`
`rm secret` in a later layer hides it, never erases

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: How are layers shared between images?
Why does deleting a file in a later layer not shrink the image?
Tag vs digest: which one is immutable?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Layers are immutable, digest-addressed and shared; pin digests and never bake secrets in.

items: A ==container== is a running or stopped instance of an image
It adds its own **writable layer**, namespaces and cgroups
`docker run` = `create` + `start` in one command
`-d` detaches, `-it` attaches a TTY, `--rm` deletes on exit
`docker stop`: ==SIGTERM==, wait 10s by default, then SIGKILL
`docker kill` sends **SIGKILL** at once, no cleanup
Main process is PID 1 and gets no default signal handlers
So the app must handle SIGTERM itself, or it gets killed
`--init` (tini) reaps zombies and forwards signals
`--memory 512m`, `--cpus 1.5`, `--pids-limit 200`
Going over memory means an ==OOM kill==, exit **137**
Restart policies: `no` (default), `on-failure[:N]`
`always` restarts on any exit, even after a manual stop
`unless-stopped` is like always, but respects a manual stop
`docker ps -a` lists every state, stopped ones too
`docker inspect web` shows exit code and `OOMKilled` flag
`docker logs -f web` follows stdout and stderr live
`docker stats` shows live CPU and memory use

blocks.title: Tip: Exit Codes
blocks.text: Exit 137 means SIGKILL or OOM; 143 means a clean SIGTERM stop. Check `State.OOMKilled` to tell them apart.

items: Expecting data in the ==writable layer== to survive `docker rm`
Fix: write to a named volume, never the container layer
Shell-form CMD hides the app from SIGTERM

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What does exit code 137 mean?
Difference between exec and attach?
Why does PID 1 matter?
`docker stop -t 30 web` stretches the SIGTERM grace period
`docker rm -f web` kills and removes in one step
`docker run --rm` skips manual cleanup for one-off jobs

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: A container is an image plus a writable layer, so handle SIGTERM, set limits, and keep data in volumes.

items: A ==Dockerfile== is a text recipe of build instructions
{icon:docker} **BuildKit** runs them top to bottom
Each filesystem-changing step becomes one image layer
`FROM` sets the ==base image==
`WORKDIR` sets the directory for later steps
`COPY` adds files from the __build context__
`RUN` executes at **build** time
`CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` set what runs at **start**
`docker run` args override **CMD**, not ENTRYPOINT
Exec form `["node","app.js"]` gets signals directly
Prefer `COPY`: ADD's extras are surprising
`EXPOSE` only documents; `-p` actually ==publishes==
`USER` drops to non-root; `HEALTHCHECK` runs a liveness command
Shell-form `CMD` hides the app behind `sh -c`
**SIGTERM** never reaches the app
Shutdown hangs 10s, then SIGKILL
Fix: use exec form `["node","server.js"]`

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: which one can docker run override?
ARG vs ENV: which survives into the running container?
Does EXPOSE publish a port? What does?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Use exec form, COPY over ADD, ENV for runtime, and -p to publish ports.

items: Docker reuses a ==layer== if its instruction and inputs are unchanged
One cache miss **invalidates** every layer after it
Inputs: the instruction text plus any files it COPYs
Order instructions from ==least to most== frequently changing
COPY `package.json` or `requirements.txt` first, then install
Copy the source last, so installs stay cached on code edits
A `.dockerignore` (node_modules, .git, logs, .env) shrinks the context
A smaller context means fewer needless cache busts
Join related RUNs with `&&` and clean up in the **same** layer
Example: `apt-get install -y x && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`
`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip` keeps package caches
`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc` keeps credentials out of layers

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Why does instruction order matter?
What does a multi-stage build buy you?
How do you pass a secret at build time safely?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Order layers by change rate, build in a fat stage, ship a slim one, and mount secrets instead of copying them.

items: Pin base tags so `FROM` itself stays cached
Keep volatile steps like `ARG` timestamps last
Run `npm ci`, not `npm install`, for repeatable layers

blocks.title: Tip: Context Size
blocks.text: Check the `transferring context` line in build output; a huge number means .dockerignore is missing.

items: `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` makes multi-platform images
`--cache-to` exports build cache to a registry or directory
`--cache-from` imports it, so fresh CI runners skip rebuilt layers
`COPY . .` before installing: **every** code edit re-installs dependencies
Fix: copy manifests, install, then `COPY . .` last
Container writes land in the ==writable layer== on top of the image
Run `docker rm` and that layer is **gone**, data included
So a database must never keep its files there
==Named volume==: Docker-managed under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`, the preferred way to persist
==Bind mount==: maps a host path in; suits dev hot-reload but couples you to host layout
==tmpfs==: RAM only, never written to disk; suits secrets and scratch data
Missing host path: `-v` auto-creates it, `--mount` **errors**
Empty named volume is ==seeded== with the image's content at that path
A bind mount **hides** the image's content instead

blocks.note: throwaway container tars volume to host

items: Ran `docker system prune --volumes` with the DB container stopped
A volume no container uses counts as **unused**, so it was deleted
Fix: back up first, and prune volumes deliberately by name

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Volume vs bind mount: when does each fit?
How does data persist across container recreation?
When would you use tmpfs?
`docker volume ls` lists volumes; `inspect` shows the mountpoint
`docker volume rm db` deletes one volume by name
Add `:ro` to a mount to make it read-only

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Keep data in named volumes, never the writable layer, and back up before any prune.

items: ==bridge== is the default, one host, NAT to outside
==host== shares the host network stack: no NAT overhead, **no** port isolation
==none== gives the container only a loopback interface
==overlay== uses VXLAN to link containers across Swarm nodes
==macvlan== gives a container its own MAC and LAN IP
Default `docker0` bridge: IPs, but **no** name-based DNS
User-defined bridge adds automatic DNS by container name
Embedded DNS server at `127.0.0.11` resolves container and service names
Same user-defined network: reach `name:container-port`, no publishing
Different networks cannot talk unless one container is attached to both
`-p 8080:80` maps ==host:container== through iptables NAT
`-P` publishes every EXPOSEd port to a random host port
Container-to-container traffic on one network skips this step
`docker network ls` lists networks; `inspect app-net` shows IPs
`docker exec api nslookup db` shows the 127.0.0.11 answer
`docker exec api curl name:port` tests reachability

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Bridge vs host vs overlay?
Why use a user-defined bridge?
How does container-to-container DNS work?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Use a user-defined bridge for name-based DNS, and publish only the ports the outside world needs.

items: `-p 5432:5432` on a public host **exposes** the database to the internet
Fix: omit `-p`, let api reach db over app-net
If host access is needed, bind `127.0.0.1:5432:5432`

blocks.title: Tip: Which Port?
blocks.text: Between containers use the container port; `-p` is only for clients outside Docker.

items: One ==compose.yaml== describes a whole multi-container app
Top-level keys: `services`, `networks`, `volumes`
`docker compose up -d` builds, creates and starts everything
`docker compose down` stops and removes; add `-v` to drop volumes
Compose makes a default __project network__ for the app
Services resolve each other by **service name**, e.g. `db`
`env_file` and `environment` inject config into a service
`${VAR:-default}` interpolates from `.env` with a fallback
`depends_on` controls only start order
With `condition: service_healthy` it waits for a passing healthcheck
Named volumes are declared top level, mounted per service
Data survives `down`; only `down -v` deletes it
Assuming `depends_on` alone waits until the DB **accepts connections**
It only waits for the container to start, not be ready
Fix: add a healthcheck and `service_healthy`

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: depends_on vs healthchecks?
Compose vs Swarm vs Kubernetes?
How do you manage dev vs prod configs?
`docker compose ps` lists services and their health
`docker compose logs -f web` follows one service
`docker compose config` prints the merged, resolved file
`docker compose exec db psql` runs a command inside

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: One compose.yaml runs the whole stack; gate startup with healthchecks, split dev and prod with override files.

items: A ==registry== stores and serves images to any host
Name = `registry/namespace/repo:tag`, e.g. `ghcr.io/team/app:1.4.2`
{icon:docker} Docker Hub is the default, with **rate limits** on anonymous and free pulls
Private: GHCR, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR
Self-hosted: run the `registry:2` image yourself
`pull` fetches only layers you do not already have
Every layer is verified by its ==digest== (SHA256)
`login` saves a token in `~/.docker/config.json`
CI injects a scoped token from secrets, then logs in
A ==manifest list== serves the right platform per client (amd64, arm64)
Sign with ==cosign== or Docker Content Trust to verify the publisher
Set retention and garbage-collection policies, since layers pile up

blocks.note: tag needs the registry host prefix

items: Pushing images with **embedded secrets** to a public repository
Deleting the secret in a later layer: earlier layer still ships
Deploying a moving tag like `stable` unpinned

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Name it precisely, push it, pin production by digest, and sign what you publish.

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What is a manifest list?
Why pin by digest in production?
How do private registry credentials work in CI?
Containers share the ==host kernel==, so a kernel exploit or misconfig can mean **host** compromise
Root in a container is root on the host by default
User namespaces and ==rootless mode== remap container root to an unprivileged host UID
Run as non-root: `USER app` in the Dockerfile or `--user`
`--cap-drop ALL`, then add back only what is needed; defaults are too broad
Never `--privileged`: it disables most isolation, exposes host devices
`--read-only` plus `--tmpfs /tmp` blocks runtime tampering
`--security-opt no-new-privileges` blocks setuid escalation
Default ==seccomp== and AppArmor or SELinux limit syscalls and file access; custom profiles tighten more
Scan with Trivy, Grype or Docker Scout; **fail CI** on critical CVEs
Distroless or alpine bases mean less attack surface
Secrets go in Docker/Compose secrets or a secret manager, never ENV or layers
Using `--privileged` just to make it work
Leaving the process as **root**
Passing secrets via `ENV` or `ARG`, baking them into layers
Scanning images but never failing the build
Shipping a full-OS base image

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Why is --privileged dangerous?
How do you run containers rootless?
Where should secrets live?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: One kernel is shared, so run non-root, drop caps, lock the filesystem, scan images, and keep secrets out of layers.
Most Docker bugs fall into a few buckets. Work from ==state== to ==logs== to ==inside== the container, and read the __exit code__ first.

items: `docker ps -a` shows state and **exit code**
`docker logs --tail 100 -f <c>` follows recent output
Run `ps -a` first: a dead container still shows its code
`docker events` streams `die`, `oom`, `health_status`
`docker inspect` shows config, mounts, networks, health
Check `State.OOMKilled` to confirm a 137
`docker stats` is live CPU, memory and I/O per container
`docker top <c>` lists the container's processes
`docker exec -it <c> sh` opens a shell in a running container
Shell-less image: attach a debug sidecar
Or use `docker debug <c>` for a toolbox shell
Crash loop: nothing runs to exec into
Entrypoint override inspects the image directly
Plain progress prints every build step's output
`prune` cleans stopped containers, dangling images, networks

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Container exits at once: how to debug?
What does exit code 137 mean?
App runs but unreachable: what to check?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Read the exit code, then logs, inspect, and exec from inside the container.

items: `docker ps` shows `(healthy)` or `(unhealthy)`
`docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <c>`
Last probe output sits under `State.Health.Log`

blocks.title: Tip: Fresh Logs Only
blocks.text: Use `docker logs --since 10m <c>` to skip old noise and see just the latest failure.

items: `127.0.0.1` inside the container is its own loopback
`-p 8080:80` traffic arrives on the container's eth0
The app must bind to ==0.0.0.0==
Example: Flask `app.run(host="0.0.0.0")`
Debugging only from the host when DNS or permissions fail inside
Test from inside: `docker exec <c> nslookup db`
Check the container's user and mounts, not yours
Guessing before reading the exit code
One-host Docker has no ==scheduling== across machines
No ==scaling==, ==self-healing== or ==rolling updates== built in
No ==service discovery== once containers span hosts
An orchestrator keeps desired state true, automatically
{icon:docker} **Swarm** is built in: `docker swarm init`
Deploy with `docker service create`; simple, smaller ecosystem
{icon:kubernetes} **Kubernetes** is the industry standard
Objects: pods, deployments, services, ingress
Steeper learning curve, far richer tooling
==Healthchecks== drive restarts and routing decisions
Traffic goes only to healthy instances
Set memory and CPU ==limits and requests== on every container
One greedy service must never starve its neighbors
Write logs to ==stdout/stderr==, never to files inside
Pick a log driver: `json-file` with rotation, or fluentd/gelf
Ship logs centrally so they outlive the container
Unbounded `json-file` logs **fill the disk**

blocks.note: max-size and max-file cap disk use

items: ==Rolling updates== replace instances gradually, not all at once
Revert automatically when new instances fail health
Graceful shutdown: handle **SIGTERM** and drain connections
Match the stop grace period to your app's drain time
Pin image digests and keep containers ==stateless==

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Orchestrate for scaling and self-healing, gate traffic with healthchecks, rotate logs, and roll out gradually with digest-pinned images.

caption.text:
Everything you need before your Docker interview, in one handwritten carousel. 🐳

From "what even is a container?" to running Docker in production, this Docker Complete Handbook takes you start to finish, with the internals explained in plain language.

Topics covered:
✅ Docker at a Glance
✅ Docker Architecture and Internals
✅ Images and Layers
✅ Containers: Lifecycle and Runtime
✅ Dockerfile Essentials
✅ Build Optimization and Caching
✅ Volumes and Storage
✅ Docker Networking
✅ Docker Compose
✅ Registries and Image Distribution
✅ Container Security
✅ Debugging and Troubleshooting
✅ Production and Orchestration
✅ Interview Questions and Best Practices
✅ Docker Cheatsheet

Who it's for: developers, DevOps beginners and anyone preparing for a backend or DevOps interview who wants to actually understand Docker, not just memorize commands.

Save this for your prep and share it with a friend who's learning Docker.

Comment “docker” and I’ll send you the full PDF.
